name: CedarDB
license: Proprietary; the free Community Edition comes under CedarDB’s own terms (64 GiB data limit, no modification or redistribution)
summary: A PostgreSQL-compatible database rebuilt from scratch at TU Munich, running transactions and analytics on one copy of the data on a single server.
intro: CedarDB is one server binary for Linux (or a Docker image) that speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, SQL grammar and system catalog, so `psql`, JDBC, ORMs and Grafana’s PostgreSQL data source connect unchanged. None of the code comes from PostgreSQL. Each table is a single copy in a hybrid row and column format: fresh writes land in a write-optimized area and are visible at once, and in the background they are compressed into columnar blocks that are fast to scan. A table can keep its cold, compressed data in S3 or an S3-compatible store while metadata and hot rows stay on the local SSD. Every query is compiled to machine code, starting fast and recompiling with more optimization while it runs, and is split into small morsels that all CPU cores pick up in parallel. A buffer manager built for fast SSDs keeps the working set in RAM and reads the rest from disk, and transactions are ACID.

There are three editions. Community is free, needs no sign-up and may run in production, but its terms cap persisted data at 64 GiB (the database turns read-only above that) and forbid modifying, reverse engineering or passing on the software. Enterprise removes the cap and adds role-based access control, monitoring and priority support; pricing is usage-based on compute and set by sales, with a 90-day self-service trial. CedarDB Cloud, a managed service on AWS in Europe and the US, has a waitlist and a price calculator ($300 a month for the smallest 2 vCPU / 8 GiB instance, plus storage billed per GiB-hour) but has not opened yet. CedarDB runs on one server: replication, automatic failover, point-in-time recovery and automatic backups are on the roadmap as planned.
strengths: One engine and one copy for transactions and analytics: dashboards read the rows the application just committed, with no CDC pipeline or second database to run
PostgreSQL wire protocol, SQL dialect and system tables, so existing drivers, ORMs and tools such as DBeaver and Grafana work
Uses the whole machine: every query runs on all cores as compiled code, there is no process per connection and no autovacuum to tune
The free Community Edition is allowed in production up to 64 GiB, with no limits on cores, connections or running time
Its internals come from more than a decade of published TU Munich research (HyPer, then Umbra), so the papers explain how it works
limits: Not open source: binaries only, under terms that forbid modification and redistribution, let CedarDB refuse downloads in some regions, and are legally binding only in German
A single server with no replication, failover, point-in-time recovery or automatic backups yet; high availability is up to you

PostgreSQL-compatible, not PostgreSQL: PostgreSQL extensions don’t load, XML is not planned, savepoints arrived only in September 2026, and range types and full-text search are still in progress or planned
Past 64 GiB you need Enterprise, whose price is not published, and the managed cloud is still a waitlist
A young product from a small Munich start-up; claims such as “the world’s fastest database” come from CedarDB’s own benchmarks

story: In 2008 Alfons Kemper and Thomas Neumann started HyPer at the Technical University of Munich, a main-memory database meant to run transactions and analytics on the same data. Its compiling query engine, which turns each query into machine code, influenced many later systems. Six researchers founded a HyPer start-up in 2015, and Tableau bought it in March 2016; HyPer became Hyper, the engine inside Tableau.

Pure in-memory systems need all data in RAM, which stayed expensive while SSDs became fast and cheap. Neumann’s group built Umbra as HyPer’s successor, described by Neumann and Michael Freitag at CIDR 2020 as “a disk-based system with in-memory performance”: a low-overhead buffer manager with variable-size pages keeps the cached working set as fast as HyPer while reading the rest from SSD.

In 2024 Umbra researchers including Moritz Sichert, Lukas Vogel, Christian Winter, Dominik Durner and Philipp Fent spun off CedarDB in Munich, starting on a German EXIST start-up grant. They released the free Community Edition in May 2025, together with a €5.3 million seed round led by Amplify Partners, and in 2026 pitched CedarDB as a single-engine HTAP system for teams running PostgreSQL next to a separate analytics database. Umbra continues as a research project at TUM.

choices.choice: Start from scratch but keep PostgreSQL’s interface
choices.why: The founders argued that PostgreSQL still carries 1990s assumptions such as 4 KB pages tuned for spinning disks and mostly single-threaded queries. A new engine fixes those, while wire protocol and SQL compatibility keep existing tools and drivers working.

choices.choice: SSD-backed buffer management instead of all data in RAM
choices.why: HyPer needed every byte in memory. Umbra’s buffer manager, with variable-size pages and pointer swizzling instead of a global lock, keeps in-memory speed for hot data and lets the database grow past RAM.

Compiled queries avoid interpretation overhead, but compiling takes time. A custom low-level language that compiles quickly lets a query start at once and get recompiled with heavier optimization only if it runs long.

choices.choice: One hybrid row and column storage format
choices.why: Row stores are good at updates and column stores at scans. Keeping hot data write-optimized and compressing it to columns in the background lets one copy serve both workloads.
